description: actionable error for a missing session id: name the near-miss instead of leaking "sql: no rows". 3 of 329 real workload calls hit this with mistyped ids and got a driver string they could not act on. Cost +0.2 kch (longer error text) — kept anyway, this is a correctness fix not a token play. NOTE: workload regenerated 323->329 calls, so 888.9 is not comparable to the 883.3 baseline; the metric is being replaced this round.

name: recall: reliability, performance and cost weighted equally

description: BASELINE under the new three-axis rubric. recall_score 70.9 = mean(reliability 77.2, performance 73.5, cost 62.1), all equally weighted with absolute anchors. Two sub-scores are hard zeros and both are real defects the old single token metric could not see: searchable_prose 55.7% (excerptMax=1500 truncates indexed text, so 44% of all human+model prose has no route to search) and search p95 1,556ms against a 21ms median. Reliability is otherwise sound on a fresh index: 100% session coverage, 100% integrity, 97.3% findability, cold index 39s.

excerptMax 1500 -> 24000 to fix searchable_prose. DISCARDED despite scoring 75.6 vs 71.1 (+4.5). The score rose because reliability jumped 77.2 -> 91.9 (44% more prose searchable), but a same-disk A/B against HEAD shows retrieval got worse: MRR 0.1427 -> 0.1302 (-8.8%), rank@3 22 -> 18, and `found` did not improve at all — the extra text locates no new sessions, it only dilutes bm25, and the index grew 298MB -> 538MB. This exposed a blind spot in the rubric: no term measures whether the right session beats its competitors for a short ambiguous query. Added autoresearch/gate_ranking.sh, which builds a control and treatment index from the same disk in the same minute and fails on >3% relative MRR loss; it correctly rejects this change. A change failing that gate is discarded regardless of score.

Rebaseline after fixing the rubric's blind spot: cost is now scored on terms a change can move (workload chars, per-turn schema, outline size) instead of ranking read from historical logs, which was frozen. Live retrieval becomes gate_ranking.sh rather than a score term. Code is unchanged from HEAD, so 71.2 vs 70.9 is the same recall with an honest cost axis (and normal run-to-run drift in findability sampling and cold-index timing). Deep-text indexing was attempted three ways and all three failed the gate — see autoresearch/ideas.md; the tree is reverted to control.

Unfiltered search ranks a pool of best-by-bm25 rows instead of every match. FTS5 resolves `ORDER BY rank LIMIT n` with a top-n heap, but the recency tiebreak is an expression over a subquery, which defeats it and forces all 112k matching rows to be built and sorted. Pooling the top 8*limit and applying the tiebreak there returns the IDENTICAL result order on 222 of 223 real searches (0 differ), because the tiebreak only ever reorders near-ties. Search p95 1189 -> 197ms, max 2775 -> 503ms; unfiltered p95 1357 -> 157ms. Filtered searches keep the old shape: they were already the fast case (p95 208ms) because a filter cuts candidates before ranking, and pooling them is unsound anyway since the global best rows may contain none from the subset — that bug returned an empty list twice during development and is now pinned by TestFilteredSearchIsNotPooled. Ranking gate PASSES with zero delta. performance 74.3 -> 96.0.

Schema v6: index a message's opening as before, and window everything after it into a `tail` column weighted 0.25 in bm25. Deep text becomes findable without competing with the opening, where the topic is usually stated. searchable_prose 55.7% -> 94.5%; a phrase drawn from past 3,000 chars of a long message now retrieves its own session 20/25 vs 12/25. Ranking gate PASSES at -1.5% MRR, against -7% to -12.5% for the three equal-weight attempts (bigger cap, windows x3, windows x40) that were rejected in earlier rounds. Also: identical windows from repetitive text (progress bars, retried log lines) are dropped at ingest, which kept integrity at 100% — they were 308 duplicate rows. Index 298MB -> 734MB and cold index unchanged at ~28-41s. Cost drifts +0.9% (896.8 kch) because the frozen corpus had to be rebuilt for the new schema and picked up 4 new sessions; that is corpus growth, not a regression from this change.

Re-baseline with a stricter rubric: added findability_deep, which measures whether a phrase from past 3,000 chars actually retrieves its session, across prose AND tool output. Score drops 82.8 -> 77.6 with no code change — the rubric got harder because it now measures something real that was unmeasured. It scores 15/100 (57.5%), so deep retrieval is the weakest reliability term despite schema v6. Built after testing a change that skips tail windows for tool results: that halves the index (770MB -> 424MB) and moves NO other number in the rubric while costing 41% of deep tool-output retrieval (19/22 -> 10/22). Rejected and recorded in ideas.md. Index size is reported but deliberately unscored: overhead is 2.1x the text held, normal for FTS5, and scoring size would create pressure to index less.

Apply outlineBudget to role-filtered outlines. The budget was skipped whenever a role filter was set, on the reasoning that the caller had stated what they want — but a filter says WHICH roles, not that any amount of them is wanted. Asking for role=user,assistant on a 1,991-message session returned a 40,381-char "outline", which is the thing an outline exists to avoid reading. Chapter density would contradict the filter, so it now delivers a prefix and names where it stops: "clipped at msg 193 of 1991 (37.4k more), continue with range='193:'". Verified the suggested continuation actually runs and terminates. outline_chars 208,512 -> 149,487 (-28%), workload_kch 896.8 -> 837.8 (-6.6%), cost axis 62.3 -> 70.5. Two calls in the dev workload produced 40k and 25k char outlines; both now fit the budget. Also includes the deep-findability probe fix (word-boundary slicing) from the previous commit, which moved findability_deep 15 -> 40 with no code change.

Collapsing byte-identical search hits: REJECTED, code reverted. 23.6% of sessions in the corpus are exact copies of another (an automation re-running one task, each run writing an identical transcript under a new id; two verified 23/23 rows identical), and searches returned hits with the same title, msg_idx and snippet from different ids. Folding them together with over-fetch to backfill claimed to remove 14.9% of result rows. The gate rejected it: MRR -5.6%, found -2. Checked whether the gate was merely attached to one particular copy — it is not: 1 of 42 sessions agents actually read has a twin, so the change was hiding real answers. Root cause was the signature: `snippet` is generated from the query match, so unrelated sessions quoting the same error line look identical. Re-measured with a sha256 content fingerprint over every indexed message: exact copies are 0 of 442 rows in real results, 0 of 120 searches affected. The duplication is real in the corpus and never reaches a result page. Score 82.3 is HEAD unchanged (drift from 81.6 is sampling in findability and cold-index timing).

Fold recall_sessions into recall_search. It was literally Search("") with the same filters — the same thing recall_search does when the query is omitted — but query was marked required, so the capability needed a second tool. Every tool schema is re-sent on every turn whether used or not, and this one cost 771 chars (19% of the schema) for a tool called 0 times in 418 real calls. query is now optional and documented as "omit to list recent sessions"; the MCP handler is kept unadvertised so anything already calling recall_sessions keeps working, verified to return byte-identical output to the omitted-query path. Mirrored in the pi extension, which declares its own schemas. schema_chars 4126 -> 3352 (-19%), cost axis 70.5 -> 74.8. No index or ranking change, so no gate run needed.

No code change to recall itself — two structural attempts at deep ranking were both rejected. (1) Exempting the AND pass from the tail discount, on the argument that every AND row contains every term so a deep match is a complete answer: gate FAILED at MRR -3.8%, rank@3 -3. The reasoning was wrong — position carries aboutness, so a complete match in the tail really is worth less than one in the opening. Reverted. (2) Diagnosis of the remaining gap: 29 of 35 deep failures use phrases shared by >30 sessions (a repeated ssh command; `ctx cancel context WithTimeout` at df 137), which no ranking can attribute to one session. findability() has always excluded such phrases; deep_findability() did not, so it scored ambiguity as failure. Applying the same rule reads 77.9% instead of 70% and lifts the sub-score 40 -> 55.8. Only 6 of 35 failures are real misses. Also fixed a schema comment mangled by an earlier careless string replace.

Search under-delivered its own limit. Rows collapse to one hit per session and the ranked pool can be dominated by a few talkative sessions, so a search for 15 returned 6 while 30 other sessions matched every term — and the caller could not work around it, since asking again returned the same few. The outer LIMIT now takes the whole pool, collapsing happens over all of it, the caller's limit is applied last, and the pool widens (x4, twice) when a page comes back short while the scan was truncated. Effect is larger than expected: findability 96.7% -> 100% (all 150 probes now retrieve their session; the previous failures were under-delivery, not ranking), findability_deep 77.9% -> 83.8%, gate found 26 -> 28 with rank@1 and rank@3 unchanged so nothing was displaced, MRR +1.4%. Latency unchanged (p50 21->22ms). Cost is the price: 960 -> 1299 distinct sessions surfaced, chars_search +32%, workload_kch 837.8 -> 932.4, token_cost 63.5 -> 55.6. Kept because returning fewer results than exist is a bug, not a budget: callers who want less already pass a smaller limit (161 of 282 real searches do). Also: cold_index is now the faster of two rebuilds — readings ranged 28-49s across rounds from machine contention while back-to-back runs vary 6%, and a ±13 point swing on that sub-score was larger than most real improvements.

Unifying the filtered and unfiltered query shapes: REJECTED, reverted. Pooling is sound for filtered searches provided the filter sits INSIDE the ranked subquery (verified: filter-inside 26ms vs materialise-all 27ms on the same query, so the shape is not the cost), and one shape is less code than two. But unified, repo-filtered p95 went 295ms -> 816ms and 76 of 218 searches changed their results. A filter already narrows the scan so a pool saves nothing, and filtered searches rarely fill a page, which triggers the pool-growth retry — three queries where there was one. The output differences are the pool truncating candidates before the recency tiebreak sees them. The two shapes encode something true: a filter narrows before ranking, no filter needs ranking to narrow. Score 85.5 is HEAD unchanged; the +0.4 over 85.1 is cold_index reading 26.4s under the new min-of-two measurement rather than any code change.

recall emitted JSON that no JSON parser accepts. It encodes with sonic's ConfigFastest, which skips UTF-8 validation, and real transcripts contain truncated multibyte sequences — a tool that printed half a rune before dying. Five rows in a 200,000-row index held one, enough for 2 of 6 sample searches to return an undecodable body: an agent asking those questions got a decode error instead of results. Fixed on both routes in: the encoder now validates strings (covers transcripts, which are read from source files at render time and never pass through the index), and splitForIndex sanitises on the way in (a freshly built index now holds 0 invalid rows). No latency cost — p50 22ms and p95 309ms either way — and cold index 28s. findability_deep 83.8% -> 86.8%. Found while diagnosing deep-retrieval failures: 2 of 11 were not retrieval failures at all, they were the probe's json.loads throwing on recall's own output, so the instrument was reporting a bug in the tool as a miss by the tool.

maxChunks 40 -> 1000, so a long message is windowed throughout instead of stopping at 60k chars. That bound left 3.5M characters of the corpus unreachable across 7 messages — which sounds negligible until you look: among them a pasted design document and a technical article, not only the stack traces and HAR dumps you would expect at that size. searchable_prose 94.46% -> 100%, all 101,175 parts reachable, sub-score 72.3 -> 100, reliability 91.0 -> 95.6. Cost is 1.4% more rows and an exact zero delta from the ranking gate on found, rank@1, rank@3 and MRR — content like that competes for no ordinary query. Index size 770 -> 768MB, cold index 28s, latency unchanged. Note: coverage_prose slipped 100 -> 99.94 (1 session of 1610), which is not a regression but the metric now demanding more — indexTextMax (maxChunks*excerptMax = 1.5M) applies to a whole message, and this session has one message holding two 1.49M-char parts, so it is cut before windowing begins. Left as is: chasing it means holding multi-megabyte messages in memory for one pathological paste.

No code change to recall; score unchanged at 87.3. Diagnosis round on findability_deep, the weakest reliability term after four failed attempts to raise it. Inspected what actually outranks the wanted session: the top hits carry the SAME matched text — the same `raise RuntimeError("OpenSearchV3...")` line, the same pasted paragraph — living in several sessions. Recall returns equally valid answers and the probe insists on one id. Judged by whether the content was reachable at all, deep findability is 95.6% against 86.8% scored. That looser figure is now REPORTED BUT NOT SCORED: it is the fairer question and also a weaker one, and it would soften exactly the ranking regressions the audit exists to catch — I have already adjusted this metric twice in ways that raised it, so a third upward adjustment does not get a free pass. Roughly 6 probes in 68 are real misses, all competition between genuinely similar content. Also verified concurrent indexing is safe (two `index --full` runs on one file: both exit 0, integrity ok, they serialise on the write lock at 82s each vs 28s alone) — relevant because this machine runs several agents at once. Checked and rejected as too small to matter: snippet/title redundancy (2%, 1.6k chars) and per-hit format (no fat).
